9.text: SNOWSHOES, STAFFS, AND ICE-CREEPERS. — The snowshoes used in north-

10.text: eastern Asia are of two varieties, in accordance with the character of the

11.text: ground on which they are to be used. Those used within the forest-border,

12.text: where the snow is soft and abundant, are made of long, thin boards. Those

13.text: used by the Yakut are narrow, and are not covered with skins. They are

14.text: therefore called “bare snowshoes.” Those used by the Lamut are broader,

15.text: and covered underneath with slick reindeer-leg skins, the hair turning backward

16.text: to assist in ascending hills and yet glide along smoothly on the level or down

17.text: grades. Their length is from 125 cm. to 130 cm.; and breadth, from 24 cm.

18.text: to 26 cm. The Kamchadal snowshoes are more clumsily made, and covered

19.text: with seal-skin, which does not serve nearly as well as reindeer-skin. Snowshoes

20.text: covered with leg-skins (Fig. 193, a) are known also among the Reindeer

21.text: Chukchee on both the Arctic and the Pacific shores (see Plate XXX, Fig. 2).

22.text: They are bought either from the Lamut or from the Russianized natives, and are

23.text: used in winter for travel in the forests. They are very useful in hunting

24.text: reindeer on the hard-crusted snow, because their large surface prevents the

25.text: foot from breaking through the thin crust of the snow.
